slides.title: Getting Harlow’s operating margin back to 3%

paragraphs.text: HARLOW FRESH MARKETS  |  BOARD OF DIRECTORS, FEBRUARY 2027
Getting Harlow’s operating margin back to 3%
Where the margin went, what to do about it, and which actions to take first
Margin plan for discussion and decision
Presented by Dana Whitfield, Chief Executive Officer
Based solely on the company briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025 actuals, tests and surveys). The pack’s data are fictional, produced for a reasoning benchmark.

slides.title: Harlow can return to a 3.0% margin by FY2028 by reversing what caused the decline, not by cutting store hours

paragraphs.text: Harlow can return to a 3.0% margin by FY2028 by reversing what caused the decline, not by cutting store hours
Operating margin fell from 3.4% to 1.0% in two years. Operating income fell from $47.9M to $15.3M while sales grew 6%.

Heavier promotions (−0.70 pts), e-commerce fulfillment (−0.84) and higher shrink (−0.50) explain 2.0 of the 2.4-point fall. Store labor explains 0.3: wages rose 9.4%, but hours per $ of sales fell 6%.
Operating margin, FY2025 actual → FY2028 plan
Cutting store hours 8% saves $14.5M on paper, but the stores with the fewest hours already have the most shrink. The draft plan reaches 1.1–1.8% in FY2028, not 3.0%.

Five moves worth ~$30M a year by FY2028: reset promotions, rebalance labor to cut shrink, price delivery closer to cost, exit the 9 loss-making stores, grow private label. After the 2027 wage rise, operating income reaches ~$42M, a 3.0% margin.
FY2026 operating income outlook vs $20M covenant

In the next 90 days: roll out the tested delivery fee, drop loss-making promotions, replace the hours cut with a rebalance, hold the delivery contract rate, give notice on 6 expiring leases. FY2026 operating income: ~$24M against the $20M covenant.
One-time cost identified, of the $25M allowed
3.0% needs every move to deliver. The moves within management’s control reach ~2.3%. The rest depends on vendor talks, a second delivery-price test and a board vote on 3 stores.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Plan values are annual run-rates in constant FY2025 terms; see appendix for sizing.

slides.title: Promotions, delivery costs and shrink explain 2.0 of the 2.4-point margin decline; wages explain 0.3

paragraphs.text: Promotions, delivery costs and shrink explain 2.0 of the 2.4-point margin decline; wages explain 0.3
Operating margin, % of sales, FY2023 → FY2025, by driver
Gross margin fell 1.02 pts, fully explained by mix: promotional share +5.0 pts × a 14-pt margin gap; shrink +0.5 pts; private label +1.5 pts × a 12-pt gain.
E-commerce fulfillment rose from $5.2M to $18.1M as orders tripled and home delivery rose from 45% to 58% of orders.
Store labor rose only 0.3 pts of sales: the hourly wage rose 9.4%, but hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0%.
At FY2025 sales, the shortfall vs FY2023 margins is $35M: gross margin $15.3M, e-commerce $12.6M, labor $4.5M, occupancy $3.0M.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Tables 1–3. Each driver = change in its share of sales; mix effects use the pack’s margin gaps. Other SG&A unchanged at 4.7% of sales. Figures may not sum due to rounding.

slides.title: Hours are already 6% leaner and the leanest stores lose the most to shrink, so a further 8% cut would give back much of its saving

paragraphs.text: Hours are already 6% leaner and the leanest stores lose the most to shrink, so a further 8% cut would give back much of its saving
Shrink, % of sales, FY2025, stores by labor-hour quartile
The draft plan, tested ($M a year)
65% of shrink is labor-sensitive: fresh and produce waste 45%, receiving and admin errors 20%.
Managers in the leanest stores say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days.
Fresh produce is the top reason to shop at Harlow (58%). Checkout waits and stock-outs are also at risk.
Better: trim hours in the most labor-intensive stores and put half back into produce and receiving in the leanest ones.
Shrink given back if the FY2023–25 pattern holds*
The target needs ~$45M at today’s sales. The draft plan leaves promotions, delivery and shrink, 2.0 of the 2.4 points lost, untouched.
Q1 stores lose 0.8 pts more of sales to shrink than Q4. Going from Q3 to Q4 hours lowers shrink by only 0.1 pts.

*FY2023–25: hours per $1,000 of sales fell 0.42 while shrink rose 0.5 pts. An 8% cut removes a further 0.53 hours, implying +0.63 pts of shrink (~$9.4M). This is a correlation, not proof of cause. Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Tables 3–4.

slides.title: Home delivery loses about $12 an order because 70% of online sales would have happened in-store; click-and-collect nearly breaks even

paragraphs.text: Home delivery loses about $12 an order because 70% of online sales would have happened in-store; click-and-collect nearly breaks even
Contribution per order after fulfillment, FY2025, $
The fee test points the way
4 stores, 10 weeks: fee $7.99, free delivery from $100 (was $75). Delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, e-commerce sales −2%, average fee $3.10 → $6.40.
Roll out the test terms chain-wide now: +$2.8M a year.
Hold the delivery partner’s rate at the 2026 renewal; its proposed +3% would cost ~$0.3M.
Test a second step in FY2027 (a paid delivery pass or higher fee, averaging ~$9.50): about +$2.5M if a further 10% of deliveries switch to click-and-collect.
Delivery stays, so the owners’ commitment holds; it is simply priced closer to its cost.
How an order’s economics build up

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Section 7, Table 5. FY2025 e-commerce: $7.7M contribution from new sales vs $18.1M fulfillment, a net loss of ~$10.4M. Assumes sales moved online from stores earn the same margin either way.

slides.title: Exiting the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA adds ~$6.6M a year, and six can close at lease end without a board vote

paragraphs.text: Exiting the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA adds ~$6.6M a year, and six can close at lease end without a board vote
75% of the 9 stores’ sales ($88.5M) leaves Harlow; 25% moves to nearby stores, as in past closures.
Closing all 9 lifts the margin by ~0.5 pts on its own: less sales, more profit.
Contribution on sales that move to nearby stores (25% of sales × 12%)
None in pack; other closing costs to be costed

Recommendation: give notice on the 6 expiring leases now, so their benefit lands during 2027. Run the other 3 for two quarters on the new promotion and shrink playbook. Bring them to a board vote in Q2 FY2027 if four-wall EBITDA is still negative.

Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Table 6. Figures for the 6 and the 3 are split pro rata by store count, because store-level data are not in the pack. Depreciation and allocated overhead are ignored.

slides.title: Moves within management’s control reach 2.3%; 3.0% also needs better vendor terms, a second delivery test and a board vote

paragraphs.text: Moves within management’s control reach 2.3%; 3.0% also needs better vendor terms, a second delivery test and a board vote
Management moves → full plan (+0.7 pts): vendor funding +$4.5M, second delivery step +$2.5M, 3 long-lease stores +$2.2M.
Downside: half the cut promotional volume is lost, none of the wage step is offset, and none of the three items above delivers.
Upside (+0.3 pts): promotions back to FY2023’s 24% (+$1.1M) and shrink back to FY2023’s 2.1% (+$2.8M).
Monthly lead indicators: traffic near ValuMart, shrink by store quartile, delivery vs click-and-collect mix, vendor funding rate.
Draft plan range: high end assumes no shrink comes back; low end assumes the FY2023–25 pattern holds.
Full plan: 3.04%. The full plan has no buffer above 3.0%, which is why the upside levers stay in reserve. Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January.

slides.title: The fastest moves lift FY2026 operating income to ~$24M, clearing the $20M covenant by about $4M

paragraphs.text: The fastest moves lift FY2026 operating income to ~$24M, clearing the $20M covenant by about $4M
Operating income, $M, FY2025 actual → FY2026 outlook
Headroom is thin. The outlook assumes the FY2023–25 slide stops, because its drivers are what the plan targets. If ValuMart keeps pulling sales down, headroom shrinks.
The draft plan shows $29.8M on paper, but every $1M of shrink that comes back falls straight off it, and it leaves the causes of the decline in place.
Contingency if month-3 tracking misses by >$1M: deepen the trim in the most labor-intensive stores, cut promotions to 24% early, and move one-time spend into FY2027.
Brief the lender in February with the plan, the tracking metrics and the contingency.
In-year capture of run-rate: promotional cuts 50%, vendor funding 25%, shrink 40%, labor rebalance 50%, delivery 75%, private label 25%. No store exits in FY2026.

Components rounded to whole $M (unrounded total $24.3M). Excludes one-time costs: keeping FY2026 one-time spend small protects the covenant. Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January.

slides.title: Start with the moves that need no capital and reach the P&L within a quarter; store exits and tests follow

Reset annual vendor terms; promotional share to ~27%

Why this order: the first-90-day actions are tested (delivery fee) or are management choices (promotional calendar, scheduling, lease notices). They need no capital, can be reversed, and are the only moves that can lift FY2026. Store exits and the second delivery step follow once their evidence is in.
Source: Harlow Fresh Markets briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025). Fiscal years end in January. Run-rates are FY2028, constant FY2025 terms, before the −$3.4M net wage step.

slides.title: Choices we made where the briefing pack is silent

paragraphs.text: Choices we made where the briefing pack is silent

The pack has actuals to FY2025 and treats FY2026 as the first plan year (the capital window, the draft hours cut and the covenant all start there). We do the same. If FY2026 (ending January 2027) has already closed when the board meets, replace the covenant outlook with the actual and discuss it with the lender. The FY2027–28 plan does not change.
The plan is sized at FY2025 prices and volumes, with no market growth. Routine cost inflation is assumed to be covered by price. The 2027 minimum-wage step is the only headwind we model explicitly.
The 70% of online sales that would otherwise be made in-store are assumed to earn the same margin in either channel. The survey (n = 2,300) is self-reported.
One-time costs other than the $7.5M lease exits (closures, private-label development, shrink tools). Finance should cost these within the $17.5M left.
Any renegotiated cut in the delivery partner’s rate (each 5% ≈ $0.5M).
Theft, 35% of shrink, beyond what better receiving catches.
Further ValuMart openings, which would add to the pressure on traffic.
What to validate before the plan is locked
Whether the 14-pt promotional gap is measured after vendor funding.
Labor hours and sales by quartile, and by each of the 9 weak stores.
Lease-end dates for the 6 stores, which set when their savings start.
